headline: Baking a unique value into the class name mints 1,000 one-off classes: goober needs 1.25 s to hydrate the page and 146 ms at the largest size, while the lanes that keep the value out of the selector never notice.

microbench.why: Every element carries a unique `translateX`, and the naive pattern puts that value into the class name, so no merger can ever hit a cache. `bamboo` at 1.67M renders/s, `vanilla` at 1.66M and `next-yak-css` at 1.64M avoid the trap because the value reaches the element as a custom property or an inline style instead of as part of a selector. `next-yak` at 818,000 routes it through a CSS variable on a wrapper, which costs 0.636 ms of lib self-time. The pattern's real price lands on `goober` at 160,000 and `panda-props` at 165,000, which mint and insert a rule for every element.

autocannon.why: `next-yak-css` at 1,308 req/s and `vanilla` at 1,231 lead. `goober` at 158 req/s and `panda-props` at 135 finish roughly an order below, because a thousand fresh rules get constructed inside every request.

attribution.why: `next-yak-css-nofold` at 0.841 ms and `vanilla` at 0.988 ms hold the floor. `next-yak` at 1.25 ms carries 0.636 ms of lib self-time for the variable wrapper. The pattern's cost gathers at the far end: 5.10 ms for `styled-components`, 5.71 ms for `panda`, 6.74 ms for `goober` and 9.00 ms for `panda-props`, each generating a distinct rule per instance.

hydrate.why: `goober` needs 1,246 ms, more than ten times the next-slowest lane, because hydration re-inserts a thousand unique rules into the client sheet. Six lanes finish between 45.8 ms and 48.1 ms. This single number is why the naive pattern earns a case of its own.

inp.why: Eleven lanes answer between 7.1 ms and 8.0 ms, since the interaction touches one element and mints no new classes. `panda-props` at 29.7 ms, `panda` at 21.7 ms and `goober` at 19.0 ms still pay, because their per-instance rule generation runs again on the re-render.

mount.why: `goober` at 1,223 ms is the outlier again, on the same mechanism as hydration. Eight lanes mount between 59.6 ms and 65.7 ms.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane at 0.074 ms to 0.182 ms. A thousand unique classes cost at insertion time rather than at match time, which is why this axis stays flat while hydrate and mount blow out.

payload.why: A thousand unique class names have to be written down somewhere. `vanilla` ships 5,502 gz B with the values in inline styles, while `emotion` reaches 39.4 kB and `styled-components` 35.5 kB, six to seven times the floor, because every distinct rule lands in both the sheet and the markup.

nsweep.why: `goober` at 146 ms against 2.46 ms for `next-yak-css` is a factor of 59, and it widens with the count, since each new element is a new rule. `next-yak` at 5.24 ms and `next-yak-nofold` at 4.97 ms are indistinguishable here, because the CSS variable is the cost rather than the wrapper.

crossCase: The Examples `dyn-fair` and `dyn-inline` shown below take this workload two other ways. In `dyn-fair` every lane uses its own best practice, which for a library with no native dynamic-value support means a hand-written split of static class from inline style; that lifts `goober` from 160,000 to 846,000 renders/s and `panda` from 218,000 to 1.00M. next-yak ships that separation as a compiler feature, so nobody writes it; elsewhere the same result is developer discipline applied to every dynamic value, on every component, indefinitely. The naive pattern measured here is what a codebase gets when nobody pays that cost.
